passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10A, Tuesday
For two weeks I have heard Gurpreet and two friends make comments about Mohit's voice and the way he walks. Today, after Mohit left lunch early again, I asked Gurpreet to stay back. He said, 'Ma'am, it's just banter. Everyone jokes like that. Mohit knows it's fun.' I asked whether Mohit ever joked back. He thought, then said, 'Not really.' I asked what Mohit did afterwards. 'Goes to the library, I guess.' I told him plainly that repeated comments someone doesn't laugh at are not banter, and that it stops today. Then I spoke with Mohit, who said he dreads lunch break and has been eating in the library for a month. I have informed the school counsellor, will call both families this evening, and will check in with Mohit tomorrow morning.
Nirmala

qa.q: Where has Mohit been eating for a month?
qa.a: Mohit has been eating in the library for a month.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet call the comments 'just banter'?
qa.a: Calling it banter lets Gurpreet feel comfortable, as if the comments were normal and harmless, and hides how Mohit actually feels about them.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's steps matters most, and why?
qa.a: Speaking with Mohit directly matters most, because it brings out his real experience, a month of dreading lunch, which 'banter' was hiding; the counsellor and family calls then keep him supported.

qa.q: What is lunch break like for Mohit?
qa.a: For Mohit it is something to dread; he leaves early and eats in the library to avoid comments that others call fun.

grounding: Shows a teacher's note on a teenager who calls repeated nasty comments about a classmate 'banter', while the target's dread becomes visible.

At the government school in Barmer, the boys waited for the bus under the only tree in the yard. Every afternoon for three weeks, Vikas and his friends had the same routine for Deepak, whose father sold vegetables from a cart. "Oi, sabziwala! Any tomatoes today?" "Deepak smells of onions!"

Deepak always stood a little apart, looking at the road.

Today the Hindi teacher, waiting for her own bus, heard it. "Vikas. Enough."

"Ma'am, it's just banter," Vikas said, grinning. "Everyone jokes like that here. Deepak doesn't mind. Right, Deepak?"

Deepak didn't answer. He was gripping his bag strap so tightly his knuckles were pale.

"Everyone jokes," Vikas repeated, a little less sure. "It's normal."

The bus came. Deepak got on first and went to the very back, alone, and looked out of the window the whole way.

Vikas sat with his friends and laughed at something else. He didn't look back.

qa.q: What did Deepak's father sell?
qa.a: Vegetables from a cart.

qa.q: Why does calling it "banter" make it easier for Vikas to carry on?
qa.a: The word makes the comments sound normal and harmless, so he doesn't have to think of them as hurting someone. It hides how Deepak feels behind the idea that everyone jokes.

qa.q: What could the Hindi teacher do next so this doesn't continue?
qa.a: She could speak to Vikas and his friends separately, ask them to notice how Deepak reacts, and let Deepak's class teacher and parents know. Checking on Deepak privately matters too.

qa.q: What is the bus ride home like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak seems hurt and alone, sitting at the very back and staring out of the window. The pale knuckles and silence show he minds a great deal, whatever Vikas claims.

grounding: A teenage boy calls weeks of nasty comments about a classmate's family banter and says everyone jokes like that, hiding how the target feels.

In the class group chat at their school in Oslo, Oskar posted another one: a video of himself doing an exaggerated version of Sofia's accent, rolling every r. "Sofia explaining photosynthesis lol" Six people reacted with laughing faces.

It was the fourth this month. Sofia had moved from Chile a year ago.

The next morning, his friend Lars said quietly, "Maybe stop with the Sofia videos?"

"Come on, it's banter," Oskar said. "We all do it. She makes fun of my handwriting."

"Once. Months ago."

"Everyone jokes like that. If she didn't like it, she'd say so."

Across the corridor, Sofia was at her locker. She'd left the group chat the night before, though nobody had noticed. When the teacher called on her in biology, she said, "I don't know," although her notebook had the answer written out.

Oskar didn't see any of that. To him it was still just banter.

qa.q: How many people reacted with laughing faces?
qa.a: Six people.

qa.q: Why does Oskar say "If she didn't like it, she'd say so"?
qa.a: Oskar feels defensive, so assuming Sofia would speak up lets him believe the videos are harmless fun and avoid noticing how she actually feels.

qa.q: What could Oskar do if he listened to Lars?
qa.a: Stop posting the videos, delete the old ones, and apologise to Sofia directly. Paying attention to her quiet reactions would show him it isn't banter to her.

qa.q: What does Sofia's "I don't know" in biology suggest about her experience?
qa.a: It suggests Sofia now avoids speaking in class so her accent won't be mocked, even when she knows the answer. The videos have made her quieter and more alone.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, Monday.
At lunch I heard Tejas, again, imitating Uday's accent in front of the group by the lockers. The others laughed; Uday laughed too, briefly, then went into the classroom and sat with his head down until the bell. When I spoke to Tejas afterwards, he said, 'It's just banter. We all joke like that. Uday doesn't mind.' I asked how he knew Uday didn't mind. He shrugged. I told him that when it happens every day to one person, it isn't a shared joke but something done to them, and that it stops today. I spoke to Uday privately; he said it has gone on since the start of term and he didn't want to make a fuss. I told him he was right to tell me and it is not his fault. I have informed both boys' parents this evening and the school counsellor, and I'll check in with Uday tomorrow morning.

qa.q: What was Tejas imitating?
qa.a: Tejas was imitating Uday's accent.

qa.q: Why does Tejas call it 'just banter'?
qa.a: Calling it banter lets Tejas feel it is harmless fun everyone shares, which hides any discomfort and the hurt it causes Uday.

qa.q: What did the teacher do the same day?
qa.a: The teacher stopped it, explained why daily teasing isn't a shared joke, told Uday it wasn't his fault, and informed both families and the counsellor that evening.

qa.q: How does the 'banter' feel to Uday?
qa.a: It hurts; he laughs briefly, then sits with his head down, and admits it has gone on all term but he didn't want to make a fuss.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager calling daily mockery of a classmate's accent banter, and the adult's same-day response.

At the higher secondary school in Mapusa, Francis had a routine. Every morning when Aadhya walked into class in her cousin's old uniform, he called, "Here comes the village queen!" and his friends laughed. Some days he added comments about her shoes or her English. When she didn't smile, he said, "Relax, it's banter. Everyone jokes like this."

It had gone on for six weeks. Aadhya had started slipping in just after the bell.

On Thursday Mrs Fernandes stopped Francis in the corridor. "Aadhya's mother came to see me today. Aadhya doesn't want to come to school." Francis blinked. "It's just banter, miss." "Banter is when both people are laughing," Mrs Fernandes said. "She stopped laughing weeks ago, if she ever did. It stops today."

Francis opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of Aadhya slipping in after the bell, and for the first time he didn't know what to say.

qa.q: What did Francis call out when Aadhya walked in?
qa.a: Francis called, "Here comes the village queen!"

qa.q: Why did Francis call his comments "banter"?
qa.a: Calling it banter let Francis feel it was harmless fun, hiding how hurt and humiliated Aadhya felt.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes do that same day?
qa.a: She told Francis how Aadhya was affected, said banter needs both people laughing, and stopped it immediately.

qa.q: How has Aadhya been affected by the comments?
qa.a: Aadhya has felt so hurt and humiliated that she slips in late and doesn't want to come to school.

Valentina had started it in October, at their school in Madrid: every lunch, when Fatima opened her box of rice and spiced chickpeas, Valentina held her nose. "Ugh, what died?" The table laughed. By November she was doing it every day, and her friends joined in.

When Fatima asked her to stop, Valentina said, "It's just banter! Everyone jokes about everyone's food. Don't be so sensitive."

Fatima started eating in the library.

On Friday the head of year, Señor Ruiz, asked Valentina to stay after class. "Fatima's mother has spoken to me. Fatima eats alone now because of the comments at lunch."
"It's just banter," Valentina said.
"Banter goes both ways," he said. "This only goes one way. It stops today, and we'll talk with your parents on Monday."

Valentina looked at the floor. She remembered Fatima's face when Fatima had asked her to stop.

qa.q: What was in Fatima's lunch box?
qa.a: Fatima had rice and spiced chickpeas.

qa.q: Why did Valentina say "Don't be so sensitive"?
qa.a: Calling it banter let Valentina see the comments as fun, hiding how hurt and excluded Fatima felt.

qa.q: What did Señor Ruiz do that same day?
qa.a: He told Valentina how Fatima was affected, said the comments only went one way, stopped them immediately and arranged a talk with her parents.

qa.q: How has Fatima been affected?
qa.a: Fatima feels hurt and excluded, and has started eating alone in the library.

Yamini ran the girls' group chat at the coaching centre hostel in Kota. Every night she posted a voice note imitating Nazia's careful English: "Excuse me, sir, may I please ask a doubt?" Everyone sent laughing faces. Yamini called it "the Nazia show".

When Nazia texted her privately, "Please stop," Yamini replied, "Relax yaar, it's banter. We roast everyone." But nobody else had been roasted every night for three weeks.

On Tuesday Nazia didn't come to morning class. The warden, Mrs Kulkarni, found her crying in her room and heard the whole story. That afternoon she called Yamini in and played one of the voice notes. "Tell me who laughs at this, and who doesn't."

Yamini's face went red. "It was just a joke."

"Not to Nazia. It stops today. Delete them, and we'll call your parents and Nazia's this evening."

Dear Mahima,
I'm writing because I don't think I can say this properly to your face yet.
For three months, I made comments about your accent in class. "Say it again, Mahima!" Copying the way you said "school". I told myself it was banter. Everyone jokes like that. You even laughed sometimes, so I thought you were fine.
On Friday, after you told Ms Kapoor, she called me in that same afternoon. She asked, "Would you still call it banter if you were the only one it happened to?" Then she told me you had stopped wanting to speak in class.
I went home and felt sick. I had used one word to hide what I was actually doing. It wasn't banter. It was picking on you.
I'm sorry. I've stopped, and I'll say this in front of the class too if you want.
Farida

qa.a: Farida copied the way Mahima said "school".

qa.q: Why did Farida call the comments banter?
qa.a: The word made the comments feel harmless, so Farida didn't have to feel guilty or notice how Mahima really felt.

qa.q: What did Ms Kapoor do that helped?
qa.a: She acted the same afternoon, asked a sharp question about banter, and told Farida how Mahima had been affected.

qa.q: What had the comments been like for Mahima?
qa.a: Mahima felt hurt and embarrassed enough to stop wanting to speak in class, even if Mahima sometimes laughed along.

Wednesday. Nirmala dropped out of the passing drill. When Coach Deepa asked why, she said, "My knee." Baljeet muttered to his friend, "Can't even take a joke." Every time she touched the ball, someone said "Slowmala" under their breath.
Friday. Nirmala didn't come. After practice, Coach Deepa kept Baljeet back. "Nirmala told me today why she's quitting. The nickname." Baljeet shrugged. "We all have nicknames. It's banter." "Is she laughing?" He thought of Nirmala's face on Wednesday. "No." "Then it's not banter. It's making her leave the team." That evening Coach Deepa phoned Nirmala's mother, and on Monday Baljeet apologised in front of the team.

Pallavi, you told me yesterday your group only does banter. Let me tell you about the monsoon I turned fifteen, when your Dilnaz aunty thought the same.
There was a boy in our tuition class, Shiv, who stammered on his s's. Every day, when the rain kept us indoors, we copied him. "S-s-sir, s-s-sorry I'm late." The whole room laughing. When the tuition sir frowned, I said, "It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."
He did laugh. Then one evening I saw him at the bus stop in the rain, practising "sorry" under his breath again and again, so he wouldn't be copied the next day. His face looked nothing like laughing.
The next day I stopped, and I told the others why. Two of them stopped too. So, Pallavi, what does the one your group jokes about do when you're not looking?

qa.q: What did Dilnaz say when the tuition sir frowned?
qa.a: "It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."

qa.q: Why did "banter" feel like the right word to young Dilnaz?
qa.a: The word let young Dilnaz feel comfortable and blameless: it made the copying sound like shared fun, and Shiv's laugh seemed to prove nobody was hurt.

qa.q: What turned things around in the story?
qa.a: Seeing Shiv practising "sorry" alone at the bus stop showed what the label was hiding; Dilnaz stopped the next day and told the others why, and two of them followed.

qa.q: How did the "banter" look from Shiv's side?
qa.a: For Shiv it seems to have been daily mockery he had to prepare against, and his laugh in class probably covered how much it hurt.

grounding: An elder recalls calling repeated mocking of a classmate "banter", a label that hid how the target felt.
